title: What is behind this link?
instruction: Each sentence describes two things that go together. Sort them by what is most likely behind it. Careful: only one box means a real cause.
buckets: A cause, checked by an experiment

items.text: On days when more ice cream is sold, more people drown.
items.why: Both are caused by hot weather. Ice cream doesn’t drown anyone.

items.text: Children with bigger shoe sizes read faster.
items.why: The third thing is age. Older children have bigger feet and read more.

items.text: An app randomly showed half of 50,000 people a green button and the other half a blue one. 12% more people clicked the green one.
items.why: Random splitting is an experiment (an A/B test). Otherwise the two groups are the same, so the colour makes the difference.

items.text: People who often go to the doctor are more often ill.
items.why: The doctor doesn’t cause the illness. The illness is the reason they go there.

items.text: Towns with more police officers have more crime.
items.why: Where there is more crime, the town hires more police officers. The cause runs the opposite way to what the sentence suggests.

items.text: For years, the number of computer science doctorates in the USA and the number of bee colonies rose and fell together.
items.why: When you compare thousands of pairs of series, some will look alike purely by chance. That is exactly how the examples on the Spurious Correlations website come about.

items.text: Out of 200 tracked facts about your gaming, one showed that you win more on days with the letter “t” in their name.
items.why: Out of 200 tests, a few will “come out” just by chance. Without checking again on different data, it means nothing.

items.text: A school randomly drew which classes would start their first lesson 30 minutes later. The drawn classes were late less often over the term.
items.why: The draw decided who got the change, so the classes don’t differ in any other way. The later start caused the difference.

debrief: A link has four possible explanations: a cause, a hidden third thing, the reverse direction and chance. A cause is mainly proved honestly by an experiment with random splitting. When an experiment isn’t possible, look for a third thing and ask how many pairs someone dug through before finding the “interesting” one.
